title: Swedish literature begins on a 9th-century stone carved with about 760 runes

cover.alt: The Rök runestone, a tall pale slab covered in carved runes, standing under a wooden shelter with a shingled pyramid roof in open Swedish farmland.

body: In the early 9th century a father named Varinn raised a stone at Rök in Östergötland, Sweden, in memory of his dead son. He covered five sides of it with around 760 characters, the longest known runic inscription in stone, and it is counted as the first known piece of written Swedish literature. It is partly a puzzle on purpose: Varinn switches between everyday runes, an older runic alphabet and special cipher runes, and part of the text is encrypted by shifting letters. Scholars still argue over what its riddling verses mean. Found built into a church wall in the 19th century, it now stands beside that church under its own roof.

slides.text: In memory of Vámóðr stand these runes. And Varinn coloured them, the father, in memory of his dead son.

slides.alt: Close view of the back of the Rök runestone: rows of runes painted dark red run up the grey granite face, with a band of different runes along the bottom.
slides.caption: The back of the stone. The line along the bottom is in the older Elder Futhark runes.

slides.heading: Four ways of writing on one stone
items: Short-twig runes of the Younger Futhark

slides.question: One verse describes Theodoric ‘the bold’ sitting armed on his horse. What is it probably about?
slides.explanation: The lines probably concern the famous statue of Theodoric sitting on his horse in Ravenna, Italy, a very long way from Östergötland in Sweden, where the stone stands.

slides.prompt: In 2020, researchers from three Swedish universities offered a new reading of the riddles. What did they think the stone was about?
slides.detail: They linked it to Fimbulwinter, the great winter of Norse myth, after the extreme weather of 535–536. It is one hypothesis among several.
